# The two armed men on the dock

## Short answer

Their posture says they are **heading toward the moored boat — walking down the bank onto the jetty in order to board it and leave by water.** They are not coming away from the vessel, not patrolling the quay, and not moving to confront anyone: they are on their way to embark, and the whole arrangement of the group reads as a party going aboard.

## The evidence in their bodies

**They face the boat, not away from it.** Both men are turned to the left in the picture — the direction in which the plank jetty and the moored sailing barge lie. The moored vessel is on their left hand; the rising bank, the farmhouse and the village are behind them on their right. Their line of travel points at the water.

**Their packs are on their backs, and their backs are toward the village.** Each man carries a large, round, hatched bundle — a soldier's or traveller's knapsack — strapped high across his shoulders. Because the bundles sit on the side away from the boat, the figures are unambiguously seen from behind-and-side, walking boatward. The second man is bent so far forward under his load that his head is dropped almost level with his shoulders; his back is rounded and nearly horizontal.

**Both are caught mid-stride, leaning forward into the walk.** The torsos are pitched forward off the vertical, the rear leg is extended well behind with the heel coming up, and the leading leg is planted ahead and downhill. This is the engraver's shorthand for sustained, purposeful, weight-bearing walking — trudging under a load — rather than standing, loitering or strolling. The forward pitch also reflects the ground: the bank falls away from right to left toward the waterline, so they are descending a slope, and their bodies are braced against that descent.

**Their long weapons are carried, not readied.** Each man has a pike or long spear sloping up over the shoulder, the point raised high into the air and angled backward, the butt carried low and forward. That is the marching or travelling carry, the way a man moves a pole-arm from place to place. Nothing is levelled, couched or brought to guard, so no threat or action is implied — only transit.

## What the surrounding figures confirm

**A man is beckoning them from the jetty.** Just ahead of them, at the landward end of the planking, stands a figure in a long gown and hat. He faces the boat, has stepped forward onto the jetty with one foot, carries a round basket or bundle in his lowered hand, and throws his other arm high in a hailing or pointing gesture toward the vessel. He looks like a passenger or a master of the party going aboard and signalling to the boat's crew — and his gesture sets the direction the whole group is moving in.

**More armed men are following on behind.** Further up the slope, on the road running down from the houses, two additional figures are drawn with exactly the same silhouette — bulky pack, pike shouldered point-up and angled back, body leaning forward — and they too are walking leftward, downhill. The two men on the dock are therefore the leading pair of a small file of armed men coming down off the road to the landing place. Nearby a figure leads a pack animal down the same slope, and a dog runs along it.

**The boat is being made ready.** At the jetty the barge lies with its mast up and its yard and sail brailed in, cargo heaped amidships, and a crewman standing forward handling gear — a vessel about to be loaded and cast off, not one long abandoned at its mooring.

## The reading

Put together, the posture tells a small story of embarkation. These are soldiers or armed travellers with their kit on their backs, marching down from the village along the shore road, following a gowned companion who is already signalling to the boat, with more of their company coming behind them. Their forward-leaning, loaded, downhill stride and their shouldered pikes all point the same way: toward the little jetty and the waiting barge. They are headed for the boat, to go aboard and continue their journey by river.
